title: Why You Shouldn't Let Your Students Decide The Class Rules the-class-rules/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin argues against the popular strategy of guiding students to 'co-create' class rules for a sense of ownership, contending it actually undermines a teacher's leadership presence. He explains that positioning oneself as a partner in deciding classroom direction signals that rules are negotiable, which invites arguments over enforcement and reluctance to accept consequences—particularly among difficult students who will test any perceived opening. He distinguishes this from giving students real choices on matters unrelated to core classroom direction, like which game to play or where to hold a lesson. The article's throughline is that teacher and student responsibilities are distinct, and confusing them creates problems; presenting rules as non-negotiable boundaries that protect students' right to learn instead establishes the teacher as a trustworthy, compassionate leader.
points: Letting students co-create class rules can unintentionally signal that classroom direction is negotiable.
This perceived negotiability increases arguments over what counts as breaking a rule and resistance to consequences.
Difficult students especially will exploit any sense that rules are open to debate.
Genuine student choice should be reserved for matters unrelated to core classroom direction (which game, indoor vs. outdoor, order of activities).
Presenting rules as non-negotiable, protective boundaries positions the teacher as a compassionate leader worth following.
quotes: Allowing students to come up with the class rules is a common strategy.
Well, the problem with the strategy is that it can undermine your leadership presence.
You see, if in any way you communicate that you’re in partnership with your students when determining the direction of your classroom, it will weaken your authority.
This view of teacher as partner tends to be especially problematic with difficult students, who are quick to fill any void you leave them.
Having a teacher students trust to be at the helm from morning bell to dismissal has a calming effect on the tone and tenor of your classroom.
The truth is, you and your students have distinctly different responsibilities. Problems large and small arise when those responsibilities become confused or intertwined.

By presenting your rules as non-negotiable boundaries that you put into place for the express purpose of protecting their right to learn and enjoy school, you establish yourself as a compassionate leader who puts their interests first.
